Azam Taufik Mohd DinPersonal Care ProductPersonal care products (PCP) are a class of common chemical items used for a variety of purposes, such as cleaning, nutrition, and beauty. Personal care products included cosmetics, skin care, hair care, household cleaners, and perfumes. Many individuals throughout the world use skincare and personal care products contributes significantly to their frequent discharge into the environment (Khan et al., 2021b). PCP is also utilized in products like deodorants, hair colors, hormones, lipsticks, moisturizers, shampoos, and toothpastes to improve the quality of daily living (Daughton and Jones-Lepp, 2018; Patel et al., 2019).Most of these compounds are bioactive and are classified based on their capacity for bioaccumulation and retention, endangering both human health and the environment. The exponential growth in the consumption of a wide range of commodities, such as prettiness and personal care, is reflected in the exponential growth in the number of developing toxins released into the environment every day (Sharma et al., 2019). Skin care products commonly include emerging pollutants, which may reach harmful levels for the general public (Kasprzyk-hordern et al., 2009; Juliano and Magrini, 2017; Reid et al., 2019). A list of developing contaminants is provided in Table 1 along with concentration detected from personal care products.The largest concentrations of newly discovered pollutants were found in cosmetics, with nanoparticles of ZnO and TiO2 emerging as significant potential contaminants (Priya et al., 2022). The following developing contaminants are most likely to be found in personal care products: TiO2 nanoparticles, insect repellents, microplastics, UV filters, and hydroxytoluene-containing disinfectants, tonalide, phantolide, and galaxolidecelestolide-containing fragrances, as well as preservatives such as diethyl phthalate, ZnO nanoparticles, methoxycinnamate, octinoxate benzophenone, methyl paraben, ethyl paraben, propyl paraben, and butyl paraben (Montes-grajales et al., 2017; Česen et al., 2019; Álvarez-González et al., 2023). DEET from insect repellents was the most often found EC, with an average concentration of about 50 ng/L in both surface water and groundwater, as reported by Selak et al. So people now pay special attention to skin and body care and personal care products such as face wash, face cream, body lotion, hair oil, aftershave, shaving gel, hand cream, foot cream, perfume and so forth. Mondal15.5 Textiles as support to personal carePersonal care products are essential for all age groups. These products include diapers, wipes, training pants for kids, feminine hygiene products like sanitary pads, sanitary towels, tampons and panty liners/shields, adult incontinence products, compatible textiles for skin lesions and bedsore prevention for geriatric and disabled persons and so on. Different attributes of the personal care textiles are discussed below.15.5.1 Performance attributes for personal careAs personal care products come in contact with skin, they need to have health protection and effectiveness attributes (Benedetti, 2011). Factors such as water or saline absorption ability, mechanical strength, comfortability or breathability, barrier performance, antimicrobial properties and environmental response are also considered for performance (Jassal, 2011). Various personal care products like baby diapers, wipes, feminine hygiene products and adult incontinence products are made of nonwoven materials. Nonwoven fabrics are made by interlocking networks or layers of fibres, filament, or filamentary structures. They are flat, flexible and porous sheet-like structures. Generally, there are two categories of nonwoven fabrics—disposables and durables (Malarvizhi, 2015). Nonwoven consumer wipes are good for cleaning dust and/or absorbing liquids and wax, removing makeup, cleaning hands (Zhang, 2010). However, baby diapers, feminine hygiene products and adult incontinence products are used as superabsorbents for water and aqueous solutions (Bashari et al., 2018). These personal care textile products are convenient, easy to use and improve the quality and comfort of life.15.5.2 Personal care products and their manufacturingPersonal care products can be disposable or reusable. Disposable products can be classified into cellulosic and synthetic materials. Cellulosic materials mostly come from plants like cotton, viscose fibres and cellulose pulp, whereas synthetic materials are mainly obtained from hydrocarbons and are known as plastics (Benedetti, 2011). Reusable products are mainly made up of pliable medical grade and BPA free silicon (menstrual cup), plastic, rubber, tightly woven cotton or biodegradable polyester (Hait and Powers, 2019; Sun, 2011). Both reusable and disposable are good as absorbent, protector from extreme environments and cleaning stuff. Usually, absorbent products like diapers, feminine hygiene products and adult incontinence are made up of three layers and a fastening system. The top layer comprises nonwoven or perforated film, the middle absorbent core consists of fluff pulp and superabsorbers, and the back sheet is produced with plastic film and/or nonwoven materials (Jassal, 2011).The absorbent products are of two types: disposable and durable. Both are multi-layered, whereas disposable products are convenient to use although costly and longer time to dispose compared to reusable products. The exterior part is waterproof and gives a dry feel, whereas the interior part has superabsorption capacity to retain fluids. Usually, the cellulosic materials in absorbents are biodegradable (Haque and Mondal, 2018). Wipes are usually used to hold aqueous things and are made of rayon, cotton, or wood pulp as these are hydrophilic materials. Some are used to remove oil-based liquids and are made of polypropylene and polyester, which are hydrophobic fibres (Das and Rengasamy, 2014). Protective personal care products are mostly nonwoven and multilayered depending on the necessity of the product need.15.5.2.1 Absorbent productsBaby diapers are good absorbent products that retain urine or waste materials. This material helps to protect from friction and infection to the baby's skin and leakage into cloth. Baby diapers are easily disposable after use. Reusable baby diapers are mainly cotton made and less costly. Frequent changing is necessary to avoid nappy rashes as the rashes come due to being wet, high temperature and friction (Kamat and Malkani, 2003).Feminine hygiene products are also good absorbents to hold blood, fluids, salts and blood cells and help to prevent leakage. Adult incontinence products are usually made of faster-swelling superabsorbents and can absorb higher pressure than baby diapers. These are thin and are made using superabsorbent fibre. These personal hygiene products (diapers, incontinence and feminine hygiene materials) contain superabsorbent polymers to store liquids. Depending on consumer requirements, the swelling properties of the absorbents can be adjusted. The top layer of the diapers is made with permeable polypropylene (PP) nonwoven so that it can pass fluid rapidly to the core. Then the core is made of fluff and hydrogels, which work as superabsorbent. The outer layer is nonpermeable and usually comprises polyethylene. For female tampons and sanitary pads, the middle layer consists of hydrogels and cellulose fluff. Adult incontinence is prepared by similar techniques like baby diapers with higher holding capacity (Haque and Mondal, 2018). Previously different researchers used various biodegradable inner core materials as superabsorbents (Table 15.5).Table 15.5. Spronger, Switzerland, pp. 1–21.15.5.2.2 Consumer wipesPersonal care wipes include antibacterial wipes, alcohol prep pads, acne medication pads, deodorant and refreshment wipes, feminine hygiene wipes, eye pads, general clean-up wipes, incontinence wipes, haemorrhoid wipes, makeup remover wipes, moist flushable wipes, wet and dry wipes, wound wipes and so on (Zhang, 2010). Wipes are mainly based on nonwoven materials with nonlinting properties. Two types of wipes are available as wet and dry. Wet wipes are coated or infused with liquid lotion and packed in a way that they can be immersed as needed (Jassal, 2011). Depending on the end usage, fibre materials vary from cellulose-based as fluff pulp, wood pulp, viscose rayon, Lyocel, specialty paper pulp, Tencel and cotton or petroleum-based such as polyester and polypropylene or both. Cellulosic fibres are biodegradable and have high absorbency whereas synthetic fibres have higher strength and abrasion and solvent resistant capacity. Wipes can be immersed with moisturizers, antibacterial agents, alcohols, antiseptic, disinfectant sanitizer.15.5.2.3 Skin lesions and bedsoresBedsores happen due to the localized tissue damage caused by external surface pressure, mainly in the bony areas. Pressure, moisture transport through fabrics and shear/friction between skin and textile cause skin lesion and bed sore problems. Preventive measures are easier than treatment for bed sores or skin ulcers. Previously, sheepskin was used as cushion support on skin. A group of researchers has also proved that medical sheepskin is an effective technique to prevent skin lesions (Mistiaen et al., 2008). Another option is a three-dimensional knitted fabric called spacer fabric. It is made by joining two outer textile substrates together and keeping them apart with spacer yarns (Fig. 15.12). Multi-layered textiles also benefit from low friction, high moisture and temperature permeability and moisture absorbance (Sikka and Garg, 2020).Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 15.12. Design and development of portable support surface and multilayered fabric cover for bed sore prevention. Indian J. Surg. 77, 576–582. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12262-013-0930-4.Fabric structures significantly affect friction and breathability of the functional textile (Ahmad, 2007; Zhong et al., 2008). Different support kits for hip, elbow, top garment and hill pads are used with a portable support surface system. The support portion is filled with water or air, which is covered with a multi-layered fabric cover. Breathable PVC material is used as the water bag, whereas the multilayer cover contains twill (one layer) and terry fabric (two layers) (Kandha Vadivu, 2015).15.5.2.4 Protective textilesPersonal protective textiles give protection from extreme cold, heat, wind, rain or flash fire. It provides protection from the external environment as well as maintains thermo-physiological comfort for the individual. Different materials usage and manufacturing techniques can help to achieve the desired performance (Mandal et al., 2019). Clothing material and design have an enormous impact on the heat-moisture balance between body and environment. Thermal comfort varies based on the moisture and heat transfer of the clothing material. Polyester (PET) nonwoven fabric along with silica aerogel have shown very effective insulation properties (Naik and Rakshit, 2019). In most thermal protective cloths, usually, three layers are used for proper protection. These layers are specific for the outer shell, moisture barrier and thermal liner. The thermal liner provides better insulation property than double-layer one. Different weaving structures (plain, rip-stop woven, fleeced napped on both sides) are applicable for different types of fabrics. Impermeable fabric can provide more protection by reducing mass transfer (Mandal et al., 2012).Fire-resistant modacrylic fibre and fire-resistant meta-aramid yarn were used to produce heat and fire protective socks, gloves, helmets, clothing (vest, sweater, drawers, pants) (Lavrent'eva and Shkola, 2015). Water and vapour resistance fabrics are also important for sailing to have protection from water intrusion, wind or vapour to insert in. Densely woven materials are prepared either from synthetic filament yarns or natural hydrophilic fibres and yarns. Natural cotton fibres are hydrophilic, whereas synthetic yarns and fibres are hydrophobic. Therefore, multiple layers as membrane and coatings comprising different weaving techniques and properties are required for complete protection (Troynikov et al., 2017). So, overall, personal protective materials are prepared using different materials and techniques depending on their needs and aesthetics. Neeraj Kumar2.6 Personal care and cosmeticsPersonal care products and cosmetics are widely used throughout the world in huge amounts. It results in the continuous invisible release of personal hygiene and cosmetics products or ingredients into the environment. Altogether these impact on the life of living beings as these are bioactive, highly persistent in the environment, and can also bioaccumulate [58,59]. Personal care and cosmetics include any product which is applied on the external part of the body such as skin, nails, hair, lips, and external genital organs, or oral hygiene such as teeth and mucous membrane of the oral cavity, in order to make them clean, protect from germs, prevent bad odor, change in appearance, and keep in good condition [60]. Unlike pharmaceutical drugs, personal care and cosmetic products can be consumed only for external usage. Therefore they are more likely to enter into the environment in large quantities due to human activities, for example, during bathing or washing and give more trouble to the ecological systems [61–63]. Soaps, hair dyes, nail paints, fragrances, emulsifiers, ultraviolet absorbers, acrylates, preservatives, and antioxidants are the common examples of daily use personal care and cosmetic products. Some of these are hazardous for health and heavy exposure of such chemical cosmetics can cause cancer, endocrine disruption, mutation, allergy, and reproductive toxicity [64].Personal care products generally belong to hygienic practices and rinse off immediately after use, such as shampoos, soaps, toothpastes, and shower gels. However, a few personal care products are leave-on products such as sanitizers, sunscreen lotion, etc. Cosmetics are generally leave-on products, staying on the skin for at least few hours, for example, body and face creams, insect repellent, cosmetics, perfumes, and antiperspirants. On removing the cosmetic products and washing or showering, these products enter the sewage treatment plants which are not efficient in removing all the chemicals of personal care and cosmetic ingredients [65,66]. Therefore these chemicals get accumulated with sewage sludge which is further used as fertilizers on crops and provides a pathway for the entry of these chemicals into the food chain [67]. Organic compounds (bisphenol-A, p-chloro-m-xylenol, triclosan, grease, fat, and surfactants) are the most common examples of personal care and cosmetic pollutants, which not only deteriorate the aquatic environment but also affect the vegetation and human health equally [61,68]. Mondal15.1 Introduction of personal care products and cosmetic textilesPersonal care products are nonmedicinal consumable substances like soap, shampoo, lotion, conditioner, cream, toothpaste, perfume and so forth that are intended to be applied to our bodies to cleanse and moisturize, exfoliate, promote attractiveness, or change the appearance without affecting the body's structure or functions (Fig. 15.1). The skin and hair of our bodies lose firmness, flexibility, texture, thickness and moisture levels as a result of ageing, sunburn and pollution. Personal care products are composed of natural or synthetic components such as glycerin, vitamin C and E, essential oils, hyaluronic acid, inulin and so forth. These are used by an individual to combat the effects of ageing and maintain personal hygiene or for aesthetic purposes (Klaschka, 2015). Cream, for example, is a mixture of different cosmetic ingredients that is applied directly on the skin to provide a protective barrier against sunlight and pollution, maintain hydration and elasticity and eliminate age spots, wrinkles and other fine lines.Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 15.1. (A) Personal care products; and (B) cosmetotextiles.With the advancement of science and technology, researchers have attempted to create new items by incorporating cosmetic components into textiles in order to obtain long-term health and skincare benefits. Textiles are the second basic category of human need because they serve as clothing to cover a large portion of the body for the majority of the day. The merging of cosmetics and textiles with the intention of enhancing the functionality and usefulness of common textiles creates new novel textiles, which is commonly known as cosmetotextiles. Generally, cosmetotextiles are high-performance textiles representing a fusion of fabric materials with active cosmetic ingredients designed to transfer these substances for health or body care through direct contact with the skin of consumers due to movement, pressure, friction or biodegradation (Achwal, 2003). Although the primary consideration is improved comfort, cosmetotextiles have also been developed for slimming, moisturizing and perfuming (Achwal, 2003). One particular example is the slimming cosmetotextiles, which are a combination of advanced microencapsulated materials and modern knitting techniques that provide safe, easy and effective slimming solutions. Thus the development of more sustainable, safe and effective products with varied health benefits usher in a new era of “dermocosmetic fashion art” around the world (Azizi et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008).The main contributions of this chapter include the overview of evolution, global market, commercially available personal care products and cosmetotextiles. In addition, this chapter also discusses types, characteristics, functions, manufacturing methods and applications of cosmetotextiles. Moreover, the standardization, utilization of nanotechnology, environmental aspects, recent advancement as well as the future scope of personal care products and cosmetotextiles are summarized.15.1.1 Evolution of personal care products and cosmetotextilesThe use of cosmetics and textiles for covering or altering one's appearance is not a modern practice (Fig. 15.2). Men and women have been using ground minerals, grease, scented oils and ointments to protect against the hot sun and dry winds to highlight facial features, clean and soften their skin, and mask body odour for centuries (Wilmott et al., 2005). Galen, a Greek physician, published a formula containing rose water, beeswax and olive oil about 200 AD, which became the first widely used personal care product (Jass, 1975). In the late 1800s, people used a cleansing agent known as lye soap, which was prepared by combining potash or lye with animal or vegetable-based fats (Draelos, 2000). The era of modern personal care products emerged in the 1940s with the widespread use of synthetic surface-active agents known as emulsifiers, which modified the surface tension of oil and water to form a stable product. Since then, personal care products have been evolving with the advancement of science and technology (Wilmott et al., 2005).Sign in to download full-size imageFigure 15.2. Emergence of cosmetotextiles.On the contrary, though the term cosmetotextiles is new, it originated from Ayurveda. Humans created fabric using natural fibres with extracts of herbs to deliver cosmetic and healing effects to the skin (Bhargava and Jahan, 2012). Owing to the rapid development of sciences and technologies and rising customer requirements, the chemists, textile engineers and cosmetologists developed multifunctional textiles that bring additional functions to garments than simple warmth and body protection, allowing consumers to extend their beauty through healthy means. The invention of cosmetotextiles exclusively linked to the emergence of modern technologies and traditional knowledge of using natural plants for cosmetic purposes and treating skin diseases (Cherenack and Van Pieterson, 2012; Singh et al., 2011). In an endeavour to live a more natural and healthier life, the new cosmetotextiles, also known as hybrid textiles, not only provide warmth and comfort to the user but also carry extra functions like environmental protection, antipollution and most significantly, health and beauty care (Cherenack and Van Pieterson, 2012; Han et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2011).As the demand for new and exciting features of textiles increases, several inventions have been reported, but the discovery of a silk thread with shape memory in 1984 is generally considered the beginning of cosmetotextiles (Cherenack and Van Pieterson, 2012). Later, a Japanese company (Tejin Co. Ltd) manufactured and marketed ‘Amino Jeans’ by incorporating the amino acid arginine in the fabric to keep skin supple, moist and fight against bacteria (Singh et al., 2011). Such integration of cosmetic or pharmaceutical ingredients in textile applications results in an innovative and user-friendly product that enables an alternative route for essential substance delivery systems via daily wearable materials (Han et al., 2020).In recent years, many new varieties of personal care products and cosmetotextiles have been developed and commercialized for skin-care benefits, stress management, hair care and treatment, body slimming and even medical applications (Han et al., 2020). Manufacturers are currently concentrating on the development of personal care products and cosmetotextiles by applying new, more refined and sophisticated technologies and using natural and eco-friendly ingredients to lessen environmental consequences. As a result, new, biodegradable and environmentally friendly products are being produced that is very optimistic about establishing sustainable markets.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780323904797000221Book2022, Medical Textiles from Natural ResourcesJahid M.M. NikfarPersonal Care Products CouncilThe Cosmetic, Toiletry, and Fragrance Association (CTFA) was founded in 1894 as the Manufacturing Perfumers’ Association and was renamed the American Manufacturers of Toilet Articles (AMTA) in 1922; in 1970, the association adopted the name Cosmetic, Toiletry, and Fragrance Association. In November 2007, the name was changed to Personal Care Products Council. Based in Washington, DC, the Personal Care Products Council is the leading national trade association representing the global cosmetic and personal care products industry.The council provides a complete range of services that support the personal care products industry’s needs and interests in the scientific, legal, regulatory, legislative, and international fields. Personal Care Products Council strives to ensure that the personal care products industry has the freedom to pursue creative product development and compete in a fair and responsible market place. Personal Care Products Council represents the industry’s interests at local, state, national, and international levels, promoting voluntary industry self-regulation and reasonable governmental requirements that support the health and safety of consumers. Personal Care Products Council has more than 600 member companies. Active members are manufacturers and distributors of finished products. Associate members are suppliers of ingredients, raw materials, packaging, and other services used in the production and marketing of finished products, as well as consumer and trade publications. The association also coordinates educational activities and supports public service programs such as ‘Work Your Image!', which in partnership with –Women Work!–(tm) provides women reentering the work force with guidance on hygiene and the importance of a professional appearance in getting and keeping a job. The Personal Care Products Council Foundation works with the American Cancer Society and the National Cosmetology Association in implementing “Look Good…Feel Better,” a free, public service program that teaches makeup techniques to women undergoing cancer treatment, helping them to regain their self-confidence and to better cope with the appearance-related side effects of chemotherapy and radiation. Personal Care Products Council also supports the Cosmetic Ingredient Review (CIR), a program it helped establish in 1976, which assesses the safety of ingredients used in cosmetics in an unbiased independent forum with an expert panel comprised of world-renowned physicians and scientists.View chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123864543006631Reference work2014, Encyclopedia of Toxicology (Third Edition)S. Sheyda Kordjazi18.4.1 Personal care productsPersonal care products including baby diapers, feminine hygiene napkins and adult incontinence products play a vital role in all stages of our life in terms of skin health and life quality. The key components used in these types of personal care products are superabsorbent polymers (SAPs) (Bashari et al., 2018a). SAPs are cross-linked polymer networks that consist of water-soluble building blocks (Mignon et al., 2019). These materials can absorb and retain up to 300 times their weight in aqueous fluids (Zohourian and Kabiri, 2008). Due to the use of SAPs, most sanitary products such as diapers, feminine napkins, and incontinence care products are becoming thinner and lighter. These products provide dryness, hygiene, leakage control, odour control, comfort and skin health and improve the quality of life. Absorbent personal care products and urine and faeces, contained in them are in close contact with the skin, and accordingly, they may interact with body skin to induce skin irritations. The resulting skin irritations are called diaper dermatitis (DD) and incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) which are the most common skin conditions in infants and elderly people, respectively. In both allergic reactions, the humid environment under the absorbent product makes the skin more vulnerable to irritants, such as urine and faeces. The most influential external factors which contribute to DD and IAD include microclimate (pH, temperature, humidity), mechanical (friction, abrasion, pressure), and biochemical (fungi, bacteria, and enzymes). The body skin responds to these factors with inflammation, through the release of cytokines resulting in an immune reaction. As a result, the symptoms of dermatitis such as erythema, oedema, itching, and pain are revealed (Bender et al., 2017).Although most cases of dermatitis caused by personal care products in adults and babies are of an irritant nature, there are also cases of ACD. ACD is one of the most prevalent skin problems in the diapered paediatric population. The diapered infant skin is severely prone to ACD due to the more permeable neonatal skin, a moist environment, frequent contact with irritants and resultant skin barrier breakdown, and exposure to topical products such as diaper wipes, diaper preparations, and disposable diapers. For example, perineal dermatitis (PD) is a common dermatologic problem in children caused by diapering practices, products used, and hygiene (Kosemund et al., 2009).The main materials used in an absorbent hygiene product are polymers, which are too large to penetrate the skin and thus cannot cause skin reactions. The most important materials which lead to allergic reactions are skin-care compounds including botanical extracts, antioxidants, fragrances, preservatives, emulsifiers, emollients and dyestuff (Bender et al., 2017). Among these compounds, botanical extracts are one of the main potential allergens in personal care products. The most common botanical allergen is aloe-vera which contains anthraquinone, a known irritant, and allergen. In addition, alfa-Tocopherol Acetate as the second most common potential allergen is frequently added to diapering products due to its antioxidant, wound healing, and skin moisturizing characteristics. Moreover, fragrances including essential oils and preservatives are used in diapering products to impart a pleasant scent and to prevent microbial contamination. These skin-care ingredients are often small and sometimes reactive chemicals that potentially could induce contact allergy (Yu et al., 2016). Besides the mentioned factors, contact dermatitis from diapers caused by rubber chemicals (mercaptobenzothiazole), glues such as p-tertbutylphenol formaldehyde resin (PTBFR), and dyes have been reported. In these cases, the eczematous lesions are located on the outer buttocks and hips or in the upper thighs corresponding to elastic borders of the diaper. Altobrando et al. reported a case of allergic DD in a one-year-old boy, caused by mercapto compounds. Nevertheless, it is difficult to find products free of mercapto compounds, and a trial-and-error method is still required to achieve success (Di Altobrando et al., 2020). Wojciech KujawskiAbstractPharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) are a class of compounds of increasing concern because they are widespread in the ecosystem and possibly have adverse effects on living organisms. However, PPCPs cannot be easily removed from water using typical wastewater treatment plants, owing to the fact that the existing infrastructure does not allow removal of such small molecules. Therefore, it is of a great importance to select the most appropriate and efficient method for the removal of PPCPs from water.This work provides a critical review of various methods presenting the potential to be applied for the removal from water of pharmaceuticals and personal care products. Several processes: adsorption, advanced oxidation processes (photodegradation, photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton reaction, Wet Air Oxidation, ultraviolet radiation, hydrogen peroxide oxidation), and membrane based techniques (ultrafiltration, nanofiltration, reverse osmosis, forward osmosis, membrane distillation) are analysed and their performance during removal of PPCP from water is compared. Moreover, summaries presenting the efficiency of various materials applied during each of the processes are provided. Finally, the advantages and disadvantages of each presented method are summarised and comprehensively discussed.View articleRead full articleURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1383586622003562Journal2022, Separation and Purification TechnologyAnna Kujawska, ... SaeidniaAbstractCosmetics and personal care products are mixtures of chemical compounds derived from natural or synthetic sources, employed to improve the appearance or odor of the human body. This set of products is very diverse: hair-coloring, hair-waving, and hair-straightening products; depilatories; hair sprays; shampoos and conditioners; lipsticks; nail care products; perfumes, colognes, toilet waters, and other fragrance products; bath preparations; moisturizing lotions and creams for the body, face, and hands; dental products; deodorants and antiperspirants; and others. This diverse set of products contains an even wider variety of ingredients. Although cosmetics are generally regarded as nontoxic under typical or intended conditions of use, some ingredients can play a role in human toxicity, depending on the extent and route of exposure. Because most of these products are applied topically, dermal exposure considerations are dominant. For some products, there is the potential for inhalation or incidental ingestion exposures. In this article, the authors will discuss toxicological considerations for the main cosmetic product categories and key ingredients under typical conditions of use. A summary of test methods and aspects of regulation and standards are also presented.View chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123864543009799Reference work2014, Encyclopedia of Toxicology (Third Edition)A.
